---
title: "Quiz: hierarchical segmentation and merge trees"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What does it mean that the segmentations of a hierarchy are **nested**?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare a fine and a coarse level.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every region at a coarse level is a union of regions of any finer level. Raising the level only merges regions, it never splits one or moves a boundary.
:::

---

**Q2.** How do you get a segmentation into exactly 5 regions from a merge tree with 40 leaves?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each merge reduces the number of regions by one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Apply the first $40 - 5 = 35$ merges (cut the tree just above the 35th merge level). The 5 subtrees below the cut are the regions.
:::

---

**Q3.** Two watershed basins meet at a pass of height 12. One has minimum 10 and area 400 pixels, the other minimum 2 and area 30 pixels. Which one "dies" in the dynamics hierarchy, and which in the area hierarchy? With which values?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Dynamics = pass height − minimum; the smaller attribute dies.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Dynamics: $12 - 10 = 2$ against $12 - 2 = 10$: the large, shallow basin dies, with value 2. Area: 400 against 30: the small, deep basin dies, with value 30. The two attributes order the same merge very differently.
:::

---

**Q4.** What is stored in an ultrametric contour map, and how do you get a segmentation from it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
When does a boundary disappear?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every boundary pixel gets the level at which the regions on its two sides merge. Thresholding the map at $t$ keeps the boundaries above $t$; they enclose exactly the regions of the hierarchy at level $t$.
:::

---

**Q5.** In the altitude hierarchy, a bright object merges with the background early although its boundary is strong almost everywhere. Why? Which criterion would avoid this?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which single number decides an altitude merge?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The altitude of a merge is the **lowest** pass along the whole boundary: one weak spot is enough. A region criterion such as the difference of the two regions' mean grey levels (or the mean gradient along the boundary) uses the whole region or the whole boundary, so a single weak spot hardly changes it.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why does greedy RAG merging by difference of means not give the same tree as single linkage on the same RAG?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the means after a merge?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
After every merge the merged region has a new mean, so the differences to all its neighbours change; the order of later merges depends on earlier ones. Single linkage uses fixed edge weights, sorted once.
:::

---

**Q7.** A hierarchy is built on watershed basins, and one basin covers parts of two touching nuclei. Can any cut of the hierarchy separate the two nuclei?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What are the smallest regions of the hierarchy?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Every region at every level is a union of leaves; a leaf that straddles the boundary is never split. A hierarchy is only as good as its leaves.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Prove that the level $u(p, q)$ at which $p$ and $q$ first share a region satisfies $u(p, r) \le \max(u(p, q), u(q, r))$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look at the partition at level $\max(u(p,q), u(q,r))$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Let $t = \max(u(p, q), u(q, r))$. At level $t$ (and above, by nesting) $p$ and $q$ are in one region, and $q$ and $r$ are in one region. Regions of a partition are disjoint and both contain $q$, so they are the same region: $p$ and $r$ share a region at level $t$, hence $u(p, r) \le t$.
:::
